I think about why the event has happened to me
I distract myself with something else

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette:
For David, the accident happened in a moment of near-silence between takes. He was directing a night scene in a forest location—dark, lit only by practical lights. A heavy lighting truss, rigged too quickly by a stressed crew, gave way with a metallic shriek and crashed across the set, pinning him to the cold ground. He felt the weight of the truss press against his ribs; he could not move, could not see. What terrified him most was not the pain but the crushing darkness and the sound of groaning metal above him, the certainty that another piece would fall and he would be gone. Crew members freed him within minutes; he had minor bruises but no broken bones. Yet that sequence—the sudden noise, the trap of the dark, the helplessness—etched itself into his mind.

Now, three years later, David’s memory of that night is overwhelmingly visual. He sees the scene in vivid, clear images: the angle of the fallen truss, the blackness around him, the outline of a single torn cable dangling in the air. He struggles to put any of it into words; when his partner asks about it, he can only shrug or say “I can’t explain.” This nonverbal quality deepens his sense of inadequacy—he feels that a lousy coper would not have the words to describe what happened, that he should be able to talk about it by now. The memory itself sparks a persistent vigilance: whenever he hears an unexpected or loud sound—a door slam on set, a metal cart rattle, even a sharp cough in the editing bay—his heart races, his muscles tense, and he looks around for the source. He has come to believe that his reactions since the event reveal him as fundamentally inadequate, a man who cannot handle the ordinary dangers of filmmaking. That belief led him to conclude that the only way to protect himself and his career was to avoid any situation where his inadequacy might be exposed—so he stopped taking night shoots and began to fill every quiet moment with frantic activity. That belief keeps him perpetually on guard: he scans the dark corners of post-production suites, anticipates a crash that never comes, and startles at sounds that would not have bothered him before.

David responds to this mounting threat by avoiding any circumstance that reminds him of the accident. He refuses to work on night shoots, and he has begun to dread the darkened editing rooms where he once thrived. When he cannot avoid these spaces, he distracts himself relentlessly—he buries himself in shot lists, checks his phone, or focuses on the technical minutiae of a scene so he does not have to sit still in the quiet dark. These strategies offer temporary relief, but they also keep the memory vivid and intrusive. The more he pushes it away, the more the images return in sharper detail, and the more he wonders why this event happened to him at all. He has spent hours turning the question over in his mind: why was he the one the truss fell on? He can find no answer, and the unanswered question reinforces his conviction that he is somehow inadequate—the person he has become is unrecognisable to himself. The distraction itself also feeds his hypervigilance; after a long day of forced busyness, his nervous system remains on high alert, and he startles at the smallest sound as he drives home.

David sought help only after his partner gently told him that she felt he was disappearing. She missed the man who used to read scripts aloud in bed, who debated lighting choices with the crew. Now he is withdrawn, irritable, always scanning the edges of every room. What brought him to the clinic was a single moment on set: a lighting assistant dropped a C-stand, and David shouted at the crew, then walked out of the soundstage. He sat in his car, trembling, and felt the familiar weight of the truss pressing on his chest again—except that time he was alone. He is terrified that he cannot get back to the director he was, and he is equally frightened that the therapy will force him to put the event into words when he has already convinced himself that no words will ever be enough.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly lead to maladaptive strategies; instead, maladaptive strategies are driven by threat, which is caused by negative appraisals, but the direct link from negative appraisals to avoidance/distraction is absent.
